title: Scheme of Work — Mapping a Term

points.h: What a Scheme of Work Does
pts: Translates a syllabus into a week-by-week plan across a full term or course.
It answers practical questions a syllabus alone doesn't: how many weeks per unit, when assessments fall, where review sits.
Without this layer, syllabus content tends to get taught in whatever order feels convenient that week.

items: Mark the school calendar: teaching weeks, holidays, examination weeks, events.
Count the actual teaching weeks available.
List the units to be covered.
Allocate units to weeks, leaving at least one buffer week.
Mark assessment points and review weeks (points 4 and 5).
Fit the whole term on one page so it can be seen at a glance.
Build a year plan first, then a more detailed term plan.
Share the one-page plan with learners so they can see where the term is going.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

body: Purpose: a template for the one-page plan. Content: a grid of weeks across the top (1–13), with rows for ‘Unit’, ‘Language focus’, ‘Skills focus’, ‘Assessment’, ‘Events and holidays’. Holiday weeks are shaded grey; review weeks light green; the buffer week hatched. Style: clean table, legible at A4 landscape. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Sheets (free). A shared term plan the whole department can see and update.

blocks.x: A term plan on A3 paper pinned inside the cupboard door.

pts: Start from the final assessment or outcome and plan backward to what needs to be taught to reach it.
This prevents the common trap of teaching everything 'interesting' and running out of time before the outcome that actually matters.
Each unit's cumulative task (Unit 11) becomes a checkpoint on the way to the term's outcome.

v: The term’s final assessment or outcome

items: Write the term’s most important outcome as a can-do (Learners can write a formal letter of request).
Decide the evidence: what task will show it?
Work backwards: what must learners be able to do in the weeks before the final task?
Place those steps into the term plan from the end towards the beginning.
Check that early weeks build the foundations the later weeks depend on.
Do the same for a speaking outcome.
Plan backwards from a real event: a school assembly, a parents’ day.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Working backwards from ‘Learners can write a formal letter of request’:

lines: Week 12: write the letter under exam conditions.
Week 10: draft and revise with peer feedback.
Week 8: study model letters; learn formal phrases.

body: Purpose: to show planning from end to start. Content: a horizontal timeline of weeks with a flag at week 12 (‘Final task’). Arrows curve backwards from the flag to earlier weeks, each labelled with a prerequisite step. Beneath, a second straight arrow runs forwards labelled ‘teaching order’. Style: clean, two colours. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Docs (free). A backward-design template: outcome, evidence, steps.

blocks.x: Write the outcome at the right end of a strip of paper and fill in steps leftwards.

pts: A scheme that tries to 'cover' too much material sacrifices the depth needed for real retention.
Fewer units taught well outperform more units taught thinly, for most communicative outcomes.
Depth versus breadth is a deliberate trade-off to make explicitly, not an accident of running out of time.

items: For each unit, decide: essential, important or optional for these learners.
Give essential units more time, including recycling and application.
For optional units, plan a lighter treatment (a reading for homework, one lesson).
Check the plan against exam requirements (point 7).
Explain your reasoning in one line on the plan.
Discuss categories with colleagues teaching the same grade.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Essential (depth): past tenses, letter writing (both examined and needed).
Optional (breadth): a poem with difficult archaic vocabulary; treat as enjoyment reading, not detailed study.

body: Purpose: to show the trade-off. Content: two containers of equal volume. One is wide and shallow, labelled ‘breadth: everything a little’. The other is narrower and deeper, labelled ‘depth: fewer things well’. Water level identical. Style: simple, clear. Board version: two rectangles.

items: Google Sheets (free). A column for priority with colour coding.

blocks.x: Coloured dots on the paper plan: green essential, yellow important, grey optional.

pts: Schedule deliberate consolidation periods, not just new content every single week.
Review weeks are where the spiral sequencing of Unit 11 gets its widest, term-level pass.
Cutting review first under time pressure is a common, costly mistake — protect it in the scheme from the start.

v: One week in every four to six
Activities that recycle the last units

items: Schedule a review week after every two or three units.
Plan activities that combine language from several units (a story using past tenses and place prepositions; a role-play using functions from two units).
Include a formative check (point 5).
Use results to plan support for learners who need it.
Protect the week: if time runs short, cut elsewhere first.
Let learners choose which topics to review.
Use review week for extensive reading or a project (Unit 36).
Support: small-group review with the teacher.
Stretch: learners prepare review activities for others.

lines: Day 1: vocabulary games across three units.
Day 2: grammar review through a story.
Day 3: speaking task combining functions from two units.

body: Purpose: to show review as consolidation. Content: a staircase of units rising, with wide flat landings every few steps labelled ‘review week’. A small figure rests on a landing, looking back down the stairs. Style: clean, gentle. Board version: not applicable.

items: Kahoot! or Wordwall (free basic versions). Review games combining several units.

blocks.x: Team quizzes on the board; learners write questions for other teams.

body: Review weeks are usually the first thing sacrificed when a term runs short. Mark them in a different colour on the plan and treat them as fixed. The unit you rush afterwards costs less than the three units learners forget without review.

pts: Space formative and summative assessment throughout the term rather than clustering it all at the end.
Early, low-stakes assessment feeds directly back into teaching decisions while there's still time to act on it.
Clustered end-of-term assessment mainly produces a grade; spaced assessment also produces useful data.

items: Mark all formal assessment dates set by the school.
Add at least three short formative checks, spaced evenly.
Decide what each check tests and how you will use the results.
Plan time after each check to act on the results.
Share the calendar with learners.
Use different formats for checks: a short quiz, a speaking task, a can-do self-assessment.
Align checks with state formative assessment requirements where these exist.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Formative and summative (Black and Wiliam 1998): formative assessment informs teaching during learning; summative assessment records achievement at the end.

body: Purpose: to show spaced assessment. Content: a timeline of 13 weeks with small blue circles at weeks 2, 5, 9 and 12 (formative) and one larger red square at week 13 (summative). Short arrows from each blue circle curve forward into the following weeks, labelled ‘adjust teaching’. Style: clean. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Forms (free) quiz mode for quick formative checks with automatic marking.

blocks.x: Short paper checks marked in class by learners swapping papers.

pts: A scheme of work is a plan, not a contract — build in slack for classes that need more time on a given unit.
Rigid adherence to the scheme when a class is clearly behind does more harm than a week's adjustment.
Mark buffer weeks explicitly in the scheme so flexibility doesn't have to be improvised under pressure.

items: Add at least one buffer week per term, clearly labelled.
Identify two units that could be compressed if needed.
Decide in advance what would trigger using the buffer (a class clearly behind, lost days to events).
If the buffer is not needed, use it for enrichment: a project, extensive reading, a guest speaker.
Record whether the buffer was used and why.
Share buffer planning with the department so all classes are aligned.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Buffer notes on a term plan:

lines: Compress if needed: Unit 5 (poem) to one lesson; Unit 6 grammar review to homework.

body: Purpose: to show flexibility. Content: a term calendar strip with one week drawn as a spring or cushion between two unit blocks, labelled ‘buffer’. Two small arrows show the units either side able to expand into it. Style: playful but clear. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Calendar (free). Mark buffer weeks as a separate, colour-coded calendar.

blocks.x: The buffer marked in pencil so it can be moved.

pts: Schemes often need to satisfy exam boards or institutional curricula alongside communicative aims.
Map required content onto the scheme early, rather than discovering a conflict close to an exam date.
Where institutional and communicative goals genuinely conflict, negotiate the trade-off deliberately, not by default.

v: Board examination blueprint or state guidelines; term plan

items: List what the examination or institution requires: content, question types, marks.
List the communicative aims from your needs analysis.
Find overlaps: where one activity serves both.
Find conflicts: where time for one takes time from the other.
For each conflict, decide deliberately and record the reason.
Discuss conflicts with the head of department.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Overlap: a letter-writing task examined in the board paper also meets learners’ real need to write formal requests.
Conflict: the paper does not test speaking; learners need speaking for interviews. Decision: 10 minutes of speaking in two lessons a week, linked to examined topics.

body: Purpose: to show alignment. Content: a Venn diagram of two circles: ‘Examination requirements’ and ‘Learners’ communicative needs’. The overlap is large and shaded, labelled ‘plan here first’. Each outer area has examples. Style: clean. Board version: two circles.

items: DIKSHA (free). Check state and national documents for current assessment guidance. [VERIFY currency of documents.]

blocks.x: Printed exam blueprint in the planning folder.

pts: Treat the scheme as revised after each run, based on what actually happened, not fixed the first time it's written.
This is Unit 9's reflective practice applied at the scale of a whole term rather than a single lesson.
A scheme that hasn't changed in several years is a sign it's no longer being tested against real classroom evidence.

v: 30 minutes at the end of each term

items: At the end of the term, compare the plan with what actually happened.
Note units that took longer or shorter than planned.
Note assessment results by unit.
Revise the plan for next year: times, order, priorities.
Save the revised plan with a date and a short summary of changes.
Hold a department meeting to revise schemes together.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Unit 3 took 3 weeks, not 2; learners struggled with irregular past forms. Next year: add a week, start irregular verbs in Unit 2.
Review week 5 was lost to sports day. Next year: move to week 6.
Formative checks worked; learners asked for more speaking checks.

body: Purpose: to show iterative revision. Content: three stacked copies of a term plan labelled with successive years, each slightly different, with sticky notes and pencil marks on the older copies and a cleaner newest copy on top. Style: realistic, warm. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Sheets version history (free). See how the scheme has changed over time.

blocks.x: Keep old paper plans in a folder, newest at the front.

body: Compare your plan for this term with what you actually taught last term. Count the units that were rushed at the end. If the number is more than one, add a buffer week and move one review week earlier.

dek: Unit 14 of 100: turning a syllabus into a week-by-week plan — built backward from the outcomes that matter, with review and flexibility designed in from the start.

aims.x: This unit turns a syllabus into a term’s plan. It shows how to build a scheme of work backwards from its outcomes, protect time for review and assessment, and keep the plan flexible and honest across a real school year.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain what a scheme of work adds to a syllabus;
plan a term backwards from its final outcomes;
balance breadth of coverage against depth of learning;
build review weeks into a scheme;
space assessment points through a term;
mark buffers for flexibility;
align a scheme with institutional and examination requirements;
revise a scheme after each run.

why: Why this matters. A syllabus says what to teach; a scheme of work says when and in what proportion. Without it, coverage tends to drift toward whatever is easiest to plan each week.

background.x: A syllabus says what should be taught; a scheme of work says when. It is the practical document that turns a year’s content into a week-by-week plan for one class. Schools use different names for it, including annual plan, term plan, unit plan and teaching calendar, and different formats, from detailed tables to a single page in a diary.

Without a scheme, time tends to run away. Teachers begin the year thoroughly and end it in a rush, covering the last units quickly to finish the book before examinations. The learners who most needed time get the least of it. A scheme of work protects against this by making the trade-offs visible in advance.

The planning principle is the same as for lessons and units: start from the end. Wiggins and McTighe’s backward design (2005) asks three questions in order: what should learners be able to do, what evidence will show it, and what learning experiences will get them there. At the scale of a term, the answers shape which units get more time, where review falls, and when assessment happens.

Assessment deserves particular attention. Paul Black and Dylan Wiliam’s influential review (1998) found that formative assessment, meaning assessment used to adjust teaching while learning is still happening, raises achievement. The National Education Policy 2020 similarly calls for a shift from summative assessment of rote memory towards regular, competency-based, formative assessment (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020: para. 4.34 [VERIFY paragraph number]). A scheme of work is where that intention either becomes a real part of the timetable or stays on paper.

items: Plan completeness. Check that a term plan includes teaching weeks, assessment points, review weeks and at least one buffer.
Outcome alignment. For each unit in the plan, confirm a link to a term outcome.
Assessment spread. Confirm formative checks are spaced and followed by time to act.
Revision record. Check that each term produces a written revision summary.
What happens in the last weeks of your terms? Are units rushed?
Which units in your syllabus deserve depth, and which only breadth?
How is formative assessment built into your term, in reality rather than on paper?
How do you reconcile examination demands with learners’ communicative needs?
Who else sees your scheme of work? Who could help you improve it?

perm: Board examination blueprints should be summarized, not reproduced, unless permission is obtained. Screenshots of Google Sheets, Google Docs, Kahoot!, Wordwall, Google Forms, Google Calendar or DIKSHA require permission or replacement with original illustrations.

terms.def: Planning that begins with the intended outcomes, then decides how they will be assessed, and only then chooses activities (Wiggins and McTighe 2005); also called backward planning.
A week left free in a scheme of work to absorb lost teaching time, for example from holidays, examinations or events, so the plan stays realistic.
The planning decision of how far to cover many topics briefly or fewer topics in greater depth, often by marking syllabus items as essential, important or optional.
A document specifying the content, question types, marks and weighting of an examination, such as a board examination blueprint. Teachers use it to align term plans with assessment requirements.
Assessment used during learning to guide the next steps in teaching and learning, through questioning, observation, feedback and self- and peer assessment (Black and Wiliam 1998).

A week built into a scheme of work for revisiting and consolidating earlier units rather than introducing new material. Review weeks protect time for recycling, catching up and assessment across the school year.
A term’s or year’s teaching plan that turns a syllabus into a sequence of units, with time allocations, review weeks and assessment points. It sits between the syllabus and individual lesson plans.

Assessment at the end of a unit, term or course to measure and report what learners have achieved, such as an end-of-term examination. It contrasts with formative assessment, which informs ongoing teaching.
